title: Electric space heater (fan, ceramic, infrared or oil-filled): safe teardown
summary: Fan, ceramic and infrared heaters give a heating element, a fan and motor, a thermostat, thermal cutoffs, switches and a heavy cord. Oil-filled radiators are sealed: never cut, drill, drain or heat the oil body, and take only parts that come out of the control housing. Old tip-over switches can hold mercury.

steps.text: Unplug it and let it cool. An oil-filled radiator stays hot for a long time: hold the back of your hand near it before you touch it.
steps.warn: Don't plug it back in to see if it works once the case is open.

steps.text: Work out which type it is. Oil-filled: a heavy finned metal body with no fan grille. Fan heater: a wire coil behind the grille that glows red when on. Ceramic: a finned block behind a grille, with a fan. Infrared: a glass tube, often with a fan.

Oil-filled radiator: if it is leaking oil, leave the whole heater alone. Otherwise open only the control housing (the De'Longhi manuals put the controls on top). Undo its cover screws and take the thermostat, power selector, indicator lights and timer (if fitted) only if they come out with the cover, then cut the cord at the housing. If a part runs into the oil body, leave it. Keep the finned body sealed.
steps.warn: Never cut, drill or heat the oil body. It is a sealed vessel filled with oil, and the maker says only its service agent may open it.

steps.text: Other types: pull the knobs straight off, turn the heater over and undo the screws in the base and back. Some need security Torx bits; some screws hide under stickers.

Lift the back off and photograph the wiring. Digital models have a control board: wait at least 5 minutes, discharge every capacitor on it that is rated over 50 V, or has no readable rating, with a resistor tool, then measure DC volts across it to prove it is empty (see safety_discharge_capacitor).
steps.warn: A board capacitor can hold a mains-level charge after unplugging. Discharge it, then prove with the meter that it is empty before you touch the board.

steps.text: Look at what the element sits on before you touch it. In a very old heater, grey or white fibrous or chalky board, pads or wrapping around the element or wires may be asbestos. If you see any, stop: don't break it, scrape it or blow dust off it, and read safety_asbestos_check. Choose another heater.

Find the tip-over switch in the base, under a plunger or a foot. Look at it before you touch it. If it is a glass bulb with a silver bead, or you can't tell what it is, treat it as mercury: never heat it or desolder it. If it is on wires, cut them about 5 cm from the bulb. If it is soldered to a board, leave it there and take the whole board. A metal ball in a can, or a plunger switch, holds no mercury. Wear gloves and eye protection.
steps.warn: A glass bulb with a silver bead holds mercury, up to a few grams. Heat or a knock can crack it. Keep it whole in a sealed jar, labelled. If it breaks, leave the room, air it for at least 15 minutes, and don't vacuum or sweep (mercury hazard card).

steps.text: Take the fan: unplug or cut the motor leads, undo the motor bracket screws and lift out the motor with its blade or blower wheel. Tower heaters may also have a small oscillation motor in the base: take it with its gear.

Find the overheat cutoffs: small metal discs (bimetal cutoffs) and small cylinders on leads (one-shot thermal fuses) on the element frame or in the air path. Unscrew them, or cut their leads as far from the body as you can. Never bend a lead within 3 mm of the body, and keep a soldering iron off the leads: heat or force can ruin the fuse.

Take the element. Coil: unscrew the coil frame and lift it by the frame, never by the wire. Ceramic: unscrew the finned PTC block and keep its brackets. Infrared: undo the end clips and lift the tube by its metal ends.
steps.warn: Coils kink and snap. Quartz or glass tubes shatter if knocked or flexed. Wear eye protection and gloves, and pick up broken pieces with tape or a damp cloth.

steps.text: Take the thermostat from behind the temperature knob, the selector switch from behind the power knob, and the indicator lights. Tag each wire as it comes off.
Cut the cord off at the case, leaving it as long as you can.
Test each part with the meter (see the notes) and label it OK or BAD.

notes:
## Before you strip it

A working heater is worth more whole, if you have mains power or a generator to run it. The three heaters documented here are each rated 1,500 W at 120 V (Lasko 754200 manual, Dr. Infrared DR-968 manual, De'Longhi TRD40615T manual). That is 1.5 kWh every hour, more than a 12 V 100 Ah battery holds. If you run one, plug it straight into a wall outlet, never an extension cord or power strip. Keep it at least 90 cm (3 ft) from anything that burns, and turn it off when you sleep (CPSC heaters 2026). Never run one with its tip-over switch or cutoffs removed or bridged.

## What's worth keeping and why

- **Nichrome coil (fan heaters).** A bare mains-voltage heating coil. Use it at its own voltage as a dump load or the heat source for a food dryer, always with a fan blowing through it. A short length on a low-voltage supply makes a hot-wire foam cutter: cut outdoors.
- **Ceramic PTC block (ceramic heaters).** Its resistance rises as it heats, which limits the current and holds it at a steady temperature (TDK PTC). That makes it a forgiving heater core to reuse at its own mains voltage, with a fan pushing air through its fins.
- **Infrared tube.** The Dr. Infrared DR-968 manual calls its heater a far-infrared Quartz-PTC system (Dr. Infrared DR-968 manual), so expect a quartz glass tube. Fragile. Keep it only if you can mount it in a guard.
- **Fan and motor.** A small mains motor with a blade or blower wheel. Good for a food dryer, ventilation, or forge air at a low setting.
- **Thermostat.** An adjustable room thermostat that switches a heater on and off. It suits a heated box, a seed bed or a small shed.
- **Thermal cutoffs and fuses.** Overheat protection for anything you build that gets hot. One-shot fuses can't be reset, and a salvaged one has an unknown history: see Reusing a thermal fuse below (SCHOTT SEFUSE).
- **Tip-over switch.** A tilt switch: a safety cutoff for a heater you build, or a tilt alarm. Old ones may be a glass bulb of mercury (iFixit Royal Heat RS-100): keep those sealed and whole, don't use them anywhere the glass could be broken, or leave them. A mercury tilt switch can hold from 50 mg to 5 g (NEWMOA mercury switches).
- **Selector switches and indicator lights.** Mains-rated; the rating is stamped on the body.
- **Oscillation motor (tower heaters).** A slow geared mains motor for turning jobs.
- **Mains cord.** Heavy, because the heater draws so much current. The wire size is printed on the jacket.

## Variations

- **Oil-filled radiators.** The body is filled at the factory with a set amount of special oil. The maker says only its service agent may open it, and scrapped heaters must follow the rules for disposing of oil (De'Longhi TRV manual). The De'Longhi TRD40615T is rated 120 V, 60 Hz, 1,500 W. It has a thermostat dial with an antifreeze setting near 5 °C (41 °F), a MIN/MED/MAX selector, a timer on some units and an overheat safety device (De'Longhi TRD40615T manual). On the TRV series that device needs a service call to restart, so it does not reset by itself (De'Longhi TRV manual).
- **Ceramic fan heaters.** The Lasko 754200 has Fan Only, Low and High (1,500 W) settings, a thermostat knob and a thermal overload protector. It resets after you unplug it and let it cool for 10 minutes (Lasko 754200 manual). The Lasko CD08200 uses TR15 security screws and has a fuse on its control board (iFixit Lasko CD08200).
- **Infrared heaters.** The Dr. Infrared DR-968 has one infrared tube and one PTC element, a blower, a tip-over switch and two overheat protection systems, one of them for a blocked air inlet (Dr. Infrared DR-968 manual).
- **Coil fan heaters.** The Royal Heat RS-100 has heating coils, a fan, and a mercury-bulb tip switch soldered to its switch board (iFixit Royal Heat RS-100).

## Testing what you got out

Test parts out of the heater, or with one wire taken off (see test_continuity).

- **Coil elements.** Set the meter to ohms. Expected ohms are about volts × volts ÷ watts: a 120 V, 1,500 W element reads about 9.6 Ω, and a 230 V, 2,000 W one about 26 Ω. Many heaters split the element into sections for Low and High, so test each section. OL means a break. Then test from each end to the metal frame: anything but OL means a short, so scrap it.
- **PTC blocks.** Cold, they read lower than the formula suggests, because their resistance climbs as they heat (TDK PTC). Pass one that does not read OL between its two terminals and does read OL from each terminal to the metal case.
- **Thermostat.** At room temperature with the knob turned up it should read close to 0 Ω. Turn it down until it clicks and it should read OL.
- **Thermal fuses.** Close to 0 Ω is good; OL means blown. Test with the meter only: never heat a fuse to see if it opens. A good reading does not prove it will open at the right temperature. A SEFUSE has its rated temperature marked on the body (SCHOTT SEFUSE); other makes vary.
- **Tip-over switch.** Upright it should read one way; tilt it and the reading should flip. Tilt a mercury bulb slowly over a tray, and never shake or drop it.
- **Fan motor.** It should spin freely by hand, and its winding should read a steady number of ohms, not OL.

## Reusing a thermal fuse

A fuse pulled from a heater has an unknown history. Heat near its rating wears it out for good, and one pushed far past its limit can conduct again after it has opened (SCHOTT SEFUSE). A 0 Ω reading cannot show it will still open at the right temperature. Fit a new fuse of the same make and rating where you can, and treat a salvaged one only as an extra safeguard, never the only one. If you do reuse one, match its rated temperature and keep it below its rated volts and amps. It is not a current fuse (SCHOTT SEFUSE). Join it by crimping or soldering at least 5 mm from the body. When soldering, grip the lead with pliers between the joint and the body and solder in short bursts, or the heat can blow it. Bend leads at least 3 mm from the body, never at the root, and don't twist them (SCHOTT SEFUSE). Never bridge a cutoff with wire.

## What to leave

- The sealed body of an oil-filled radiator. Don't cut, drill, drain or heat it.
- Broken coils, cracked tubes and PTC blocks with cracked ceramic.
- Mercury tip switches that are cracked or leaking (see the mercury hazard card).
- Grey or white fibrous pads or board in a very old heater. EPA lists portable heaters among older appliances with asbestos parts (EPA asbestos legacy uses). Don't break them; follow safety_asbestos_check.
- The plastic case.
